gene.name: arylsulfatase A
gene.function: Lysosomal enzyme that catalyzes the hydrolysis of cerebroside-3-sulfate (N-acyl-1-beta-D-(3-O-sulfo)-galactosyl-sphing-4- enine) into cerebroside and sulfate, a reaction that requires the activator protein saposin B. Also involved in the catabolism of other sulfoglycosphingolipids such as SB1a and SM3 (beta-D-3-sulfogalactosyl- (1->4)-beta-D-glucosyl-(1<->1')-N-acylsphing-4-enine) (By similarity).

gene.name: BAG cochaperone 3
gene.function: Co-chaperone and adapter protein that connects different classes of molecular chaperones including heat shock proteins 70 (HSP70s), e.g. HSPA1A/HSP70 or HSPA8/HSC70, and small heat shock proteins (sHSPs), e.g. HSPB8. Acts as a nucleotide-exchange factor (NEF) promoting the release of ADP from HSP70s, thereby triggering client protein release. Nucleotide release is mediated via BAG3 binding to the nucleotide-binding domain (NBD) of HSP70s, whereas client release is mediated via binding to the substrate-binding domain (SBD). Has anti-apoptotic activity. Plays a role in the HSF1 nucleocytoplasmic transport.

gene.name: double homeobox 4
gene.function: Transcription factor that is selectively and transiently expressed in cleavage-stage embryos. Binds to double-stranded DNA elements with the consensus sequence 5'- TAATCTAATCA-3'. Binds to chromatin containing histone H3 acetylated at 'Lys-27' (H3K27ac) and promotes deacetylation of H3K27ac. In parallel, binds to chromatin that lacks histone H3 acetylation at 'Lys-27' (H3K27ac) and recruits EP300 and CREBBP to promote acetylation of histone H3 at 'Lys-27' at new sites. Involved in transcriptional regulation of numerous genes, primarily as transcriptional activator, but also mediates repression of a set of target genes. Promotes expression of ZSCAN4 and KDM4E, two proteins with essential roles during early embryogenesis. Promotes nuclear translocation of CTNNB1/beta-catenin and its subsequent activation of target genes. Heterologous expression in cultured embryonic stem cells mediates transcription of HERVL retrotransposons and transcripts derived from ACRO1 and HSATII satellite repeats. May activate expression of PITX1. May regulate microRNA (miRNA) expression. Inappropriate expression can inhibit myogenesis and promote apoptosis.

gene.name: alpha glucosidase
gene.function: Essential for the degradation of glycogen in lysosomes. Has highest activity on alpha-1,4-linked glycosidic linkages, but can also hydrolyze alpha-1,6-linked glucans.

gene.name: galactosidase alpha
gene.function: Catalyzes the hydrolysis of glycosphingolipids and participates in their degradation in the lysosome. .

gene.name: iduronate 2-sulfatase
gene.function: Lysosomal enzyme involved in the degradation pathway of dermatan sulfate and heparan sulfate.

gene.name: alpha-L-iduronidase
gene.function: Lysosomal hydrolase responsible for the degradation of the glycosaminoglycans heparan sulfate and dermatan sulfate. .

gene.name: insulin like growth factor 2 receptor
gene.function: Mediates the transport of phosphorylated lysosomal enzymes from the Golgi complex and the cell surface to lysosomes. Lysosomal enzymes bearing phosphomannosyl residues bind specifically to mannose-6-phosphate receptors in the Golgi apparatus and the resulting receptor-ligand complex is transported to an acidic prelysosomal compartment where the low pH mediates the dissociation of the complex. The receptor is then recycled back to the Golgi for another round of trafficking through its binding to the retromer. This receptor also binds IGF2. Acts as a positive regulator of T-cell coactivation by binding DPP4.

gene.name: iron responsive element binding protein 2
gene.function: RNA-binding protein that binds to iron-responsive elements (IRES), which are stem-loop structures found in the 5'-UTR of ferritin, and delta aminolevulinic acid synthase mRNAs, and in the 3'-UTR of transferrin receptor mRNA. Binding to the IRE element in ferritin results in the repression of its mRNA translation. Binding of the protein to the transferrin receptor mRNA inhibits the degradation of this otherwise rapidly degraded mRNA. .

gene.name: leucyl-tRNA synthetase 1
gene.function: Aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase that catalyzes the specific attachment of leucine to its cognate tRNA (tRNA(Leu)). It performs tRNA aminoacylation in a two-step reaction: Leu is initially activated by ATP to form a leucyl-adenylate (Leu-AMP) intermediate; then the leucyl moiety is transferred to the acceptor 3' end of the tRNA to yield leucyl-tRNA. To improve the fidelity of catalytic reactions, it is also able to hydrolyze misactivated aminoacyl-adenylate intermediates (pre-transfer editing) and mischarged aminoacyl-tRNAs (post-transfer editing).

gene.name: myotilin
gene.function: Component of a complex of multiple actin cross-linking proteins. Involved in the control of myofibril assembly and stability at the Z lines in muscle cells. .

gene.name: sulfatase modifying factor 1
gene.function: Oxidase that catalyzes the conversion of cysteine to 3- oxoalanine on target proteins, using molecular oxygen and an unidentified reducing agent. 3- oxoalanine modification, which is also named formylglycine (fGly), occurs in the maturation of arylsulfatases and some alkaline phosphatases that use the hydrated form of 3-oxoalanine as a catalytic nucleophile. Known substrates include GALNS, ARSA, STS and ARSE.

papers.title: Transcription factor EB (TFEB) is a new therapeutic target for Pompe disease.
papers.summary: TFEB overexpression cleared lysosomal glycogen, enlarged lysosomes, and autophagic build-up in Pompe disease myotubes, isolated muscle fibres, and mouse muscle, with effects strongly attenuated when autophagy was genetically suppressed. The study identifies TFEB modulation as a preclinical therapeutic approach but does not establish clinical efficacy or long-term safety.
papers.why: TFEB overexpression reduced glycogen accumulation and autophagic pathology while improving autophagosome processing in cell and mouse models of Pompe disease.

papers.title: Structure of human lysosomal acid α-glucosidase-a guide for the treatment of Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The paper defines high-resolution structures of recombinant human lysosomal acid α-glucosidase and its complexes with inhibitors and N-acetylcysteine, revealing substrate-binding and allosteric chaperone sites. It provides structural and biochemical evidence that N-acetylcysteine stabilizes GAA without directly inhibiting its catalytic activity and may rescue structural perturbations caused by some GAA mutations.
papers.why: The paper provides experimentally determined GAA structures and demonstrates structural stabilization by N-acetylcysteine, a pharmacological chaperone approach relevant to Pompe disease.

papers.title: Genetic landscape and novel disease mechanisms from a large LGMD cohort of 4656 patients.
papers.summary: Targeted next-generation sequencing of 4,656 patients clinically suspected of limb-girdle muscular dystrophy identified 38 cases of late-onset Pompe disease, corresponding to a prevalence of 0.8% in this cohort. Pathogenic GAA variants were often compound heterozygous, and the findings highlight both the need to consider Pompe disease in LGMD-suspected patients and the need for additional deletion, duplication, and enzyme analysis in patients with only one detected pathogenic GAA variant.
papers.why: The large LGMD sequencing program successfully identified late-onset Pompe disease and demonstrates the utility of an NGS differential-diagnosis panel.

papers.title: The pharmacological chaperone N-butyldeoxynojirimycin enhances enzyme replacement therapy in Pompe disease fibroblasts.
papers.summary: The study shows that coadministration of the pharmacological chaperone N-butyldeoxynojirimycin (NB-DNJ) with recombinant human acid α-glucosidase (rhGAA) improves intracellular and tissue enzyme correction in Pompe disease fibroblasts and a Gaa knockout mouse model. A corresponding chaperone–enzyme replacement combination enhances α-galactosidase A correction in Fabry disease fibroblasts, indicating that the strategy can transfer across lysosomal storage diseases when the chaperone has a specific interaction with the replacement enzyme.
papers.why: The study shows that NB-DNJ improves recombinant GAA uptake, maturation, stability, and enzyme correction in Pompe fibroblasts and synergizes with enzyme replacement in mice.

papers.title: Clinical features and predictors for disease natural progression in adults with Pompe disease: a nationwide prospective observational study.
papers.summary: This prospective observational study of 94 untreated adults with Pompe disease found progressive loss of skeletal muscle strength and pulmonary function over an average follow-up of 1.6 years, although some patients remained stable. Longer disease duration and reduced baseline forced vital capacity predicted faster muscle-strength decline, while ptosis, bulbar weakness, scapular winging, and early trunk or limb-girdle involvement were common clinical features.
papers.why: A 94-patient prospective study defines longitudinal muscle and pulmonary outcome measures and identifies clinical predictors of progression in adult Pompe disease.

papers.title: Large variation in effects during 10 years of enzyme therapy in adults with Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a 10-year prospective cohort of 30 adults with Pompe disease, enzyme replacement therapy generally stabilized or improved muscle strength, walking ability, and pulmonary function for approximately 3–5 years and slowed deterioration compared with expected untreated progression. Treatment responses varied substantially, with secondary decline in many patients, ongoing decline from treatment initiation in 7%, and increased wheelchair or ventilatory dependence despite therapy.
papers.why: Provides 10-year Pompe disease-specific evidence that ERT benefits muscle, walking, and pulmonary function, while quantifying substantial variability and secondary decline.

papers.title: Algorithm for the early diagnosis and treatment of patients with cross reactive immunologic material-negative classic infantile pompe disease: a step towards improving the efficacy of ERT.
papers.summary: In a seven-patient observational cohort, rapid identification of CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease followed by early initiation of immune tolerance induction with rituximab, methotrexate, and intravenous immunoglobulin concurrent with alglucosidase alfa was associated with lower anti-rhGAA antibody titers, improvement in cardiomyopathy, and longer invasive-ventilator-free survival than enzyme replacement therapy alone. One patient died of respiratory failure, and residual muscle weakness, motor impairment, feeding difficulties, and the potential need for repeat immune tolerance induction remained.
papers.why: The study demonstrates an algorithm for identifying CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease and combines ERT with immune tolerance induction to reduce antibody responses.

papers.title: Large-Scale Expansion of Human iPSC-Derived Skeletal Muscle Cells for Disease Modeling and Cell-Based Therapeutic Strategies.
papers.summary: The paper shows that transgene-free, FACS-purified myogenic progenitors from healthy-control and Pompe disease iPSCs can be expanded, cryopreserved, differentiated into contractile myotubes, and engrafted after intramuscular transplantation into injured mouse muscle. In a classic infantile Pompe disease iPSC model, CRISPR/Cas9 insertion of GAA cDNA into the AAVS1 locus restored GAA expression and activity and normalized glycogen accumulation in myotubes.
papers.why: The study develops scalable Pompe iPSC-derived muscle cells and corrects GAA deficiency, preventing glycogen accumulation in patient-derived myotubes.

papers.title: Impact of enzyme replacement therapy on survival in adults with Pompe disease: results from a prospective international observational study.
papers.summary: In a prospective international observational study of 283 adults with Pompe disease, enzyme replacement therapy was associated with improved overall survival after adjustment for major demographic and severity covariates (hazard ratio 0.41, 95% CI 0.19–0.87). The paper identifies alglucosidase alfa as the only approved disease-specific therapy and reports prior efficacy for muscle strength, walking distance, and pulmonary function, while emphasizing that enzyme replacement therapy is not curative.
papers.why: Prospective data from 283 adults show that ERT is positively associated with survival, providing direct evidence for an existing treatment.

papers.title: Abnormal mannose-6-phosphate receptor trafficking impairs recombinant alpha-glucosidase uptake in Pompe disease fibroblasts.
papers.summary: In patient-derived Pompe disease fibroblasts, glycogen-associated cellular abnormalities include expanded autophagy, Golgi and trans-Golgi network changes, and defective cation-independent mannose-6-phosphate receptor trafficking, with stronger effects in severe and intermediate disease. Disrupted CI-MPR availability reduces uptake, lysosomal targeting, processing, and short-term correction by recombinant human GAA, whereas continuous six-day treatment improves GAA activity and partially restores CI-MPR localization.
papers.why: Pompe patient fibroblasts and intracellular uptake assays identify impaired CI-MPR trafficking as a measurable mechanism of reduced response to recombinant GAA enzyme replacement therapy.

papers.title: Long term clinical history of an Italian cohort of infantile onset Pompe disease treated with enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 28 infants with infantile-onset Pompe disease, alglucosidase alfa enzyme replacement therapy was associated with improved survival and cardiac normalization, especially in CRIM-positive patients, but did not prevent progressive motor, respiratory, feeding, or central nervous system deterioration. Immunomodulation, desensitization, and modified dosing strategies were used for individual complications, but the evidence for durable benefit was limited.
papers.why: This multicenter cohort provides long-term real-world efficacy and prognostic data for ERT in infantile Pompe disease, including functional outcomes and CRIM-associated survival differences.

papers.title: Pompe Disease: a Clinical, Diagnostic, and Therapeutic Overview.
papers.summary: This review identifies acid alpha-glucosidase deficiency as the cause of Pompe disease and summarizes enzyme assays, genetic testing, newborn screening, supportive care, and current and investigational therapies. Enzyme replacement therapy improves survival, cardiac function, and muscle outcomes initially, but its benefit wanes after 2–3 years; newer enzyme formulations were non-inferior rather than superior to alglucosidase alfa, while gene therapy, substrate reduction, and improved outcome measures remain investigational.
papers.why: This review summarizes multiple clinically available or clinically tested diagnostic and therapeutic approaches for Pompe disease.

papers.title: CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease: characterization of immune responses in patients treated with ERT monotherapy.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 20 CRIM-negative patients with infantile Pompe disease receiving alglucosidase alfa monotherapy, 85% developed clinically significant anti-recombinant human GAA IgG antibodies, and high sustained titers were associated with invasive ventilation and death. GAA genotype, particularly nonsense mutations, was associated with antibody-response severity, while early initiation of ERT alone did not reliably prevent immune responses.
papers.why: The study provides patient data identifying anti-drug antibody titers and genotype-associated immune-response phenotypes relevant to ERT monitoring and immune-tolerance strategies.

papers.title: The clinical relevance of outcomes used in late-onset Pompe disease: can we do better?
papers.summary: This review analyzes the clinical relevance of 6-minute walking test distance and forced vital capacity in late-onset Pompe disease by applying minimal clinically important differences derived from chronic respiratory diseases. Most reviewed alglucosidase alfa studies reported 6MWT changes within or above extrapolated MCID ranges, while FVC results were mixed; the authors recommend disease-specific validation and alternative measures including SNIP, MIP, MEP, GSCG, and R-PAct.
papers.why: The review evaluates existing functional and respiratory endpoints and provides methodological guidance for interpreting and improving Pompe disease outcomes.

papers.title: The humanistic burden of Pompe disease: are there still unmet needs? A systematic review.
papers.summary: This systematic review finds that late-onset Pompe disease remains associated with substantial impairment of health-related quality of life, activities of daily living, symptom burden, and caregiver well-being even after enzyme-replacement therapy. Recombinant human acid α-glucosidase provides short-term stabilization and modest benefits but does not normalize long-term outcomes, while evidence for infantile-onset disease, treatment satisfaction, adherence, and caregiver response to treatment remains limited.
papers.why: The systematic review identifies validated patient-centered outcome domains and instruments for quantifying Pompe disease burden and treatment impact.

papers.title: Transforming the clinical outcome in CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease identified via newborn screening: the benefits of early treatment with enzyme replacement therapy and immune tolerance induction.
papers.summary: In this retrospective international pediatric cohort, early initiation of enzyme replacement therapy plus prophylactic immune tolerance induction with rituximab, methotrexate, and IVIG in CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease was associated with improved survival, respiratory and feeding outcomes, cardiac measurements, motor development, muscle-damage biomarkers, and maintenance of immune tolerance to ERT. The strongest results occurred when treatment began within the first four weeks of life, but the early-treatment group was small and relatively young at follow-up.
papers.why: The study reports improved cardiac, motor, pulmonary, and biomarker outcomes when ERT and immune tolerance induction are initiated early in CRIM-negative infantile Pompe disease.

papers.title: The First Year Experience of Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease in California.
papers.summary: California’s first year of universal newborn screening identified 18Pompe disease cases among 453,152 newborns using a two-tier workflow of GAA enzyme activity measurement and GAA gene sequencing, with confirmatory biochemical, molecular, urine Hex4, and clinical evaluation. The study also describes ERT use in two infantile-onset cases, but short follow-up and uncertainty surrounding variants of uncertain significance prevented assessment of treatment outcomes and definitive classification of some suspected late-onset cases.
papers.why: This large implementation study validates a two-tier newborn-screening workflow for Pompe disease and provides detailed diagnostic performance and follow-up data.

papers.title: Targeted approaches to induce immune tolerance for Pompe disease therapy.
papers.summary: This review describes approaches to improve enzyme replacement therapy and gene therapy for Pompe disease by reducing immune responses against GAA and viral vectors. Pharmacological chaperones, GILT-tagged GAA, immune-suppressive drugs, and antigen-specific tolerance strategies including oral, erythrocyte, hematopoietic stem-cell, and liver-directed delivery showed promise, but the evidence was mainly preclinical or early clinical and no universally accepted immune-management standard had been adopted.
papers.why: This review identifies clinically or preclinically tested approaches for inducing immune tolerance to GAA enzyme and gene therapies in Pompe disease.

papers.title: A genetic modifier of symptom onset in Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The study identifies synonymous GAA variant c.510C>T on the c.-32-13T>G (IVS1) allele as a genetic modifier that worsens aberrant pre-mRNA splicing, lowers residual GAA enzyme activity, and is associated with earlier or more frequent symptomatic Pompe disease. The findings support including c.510C>T analysis in newborn screening and routine DNA diagnostics to help estimate symptom onset and inform the timing of enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.why: The study identifies and functionally validates a genetic modifier that can improve prediction of symptom onset in patients carrying the Pompe-associated IVS1 allele.

papers.title: Lung MRI and impairment of diaphragmatic function in Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a cross-sectional study of ten adults with Pompe disease, lung MRI showed markedly impaired diaphragmatic displacement that correlated strongly with supine forced vital capacity and postural drop. The findings support lung MRI as a tool for detailed assessment of diaphragmatic and chest-wall dysfunction, although the small, selected cohort and MRI contraindications limit generalizability.
papers.why: Lung MRI is tested in Pompe patients and volunteers as a quantitative method for visualizing and measuring diaphragmatic and chest-wall dysfunction.

papers.title: Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease: Pennsylvania Experience.
papers.summary: Pennsylvania newborn screening combined dried-blood-spot GAA enzyme activity measured by FIA/MS/MS with second-tier full GAA sequencing, identifying 2 cases of infantile-onset Pompe disease, 31 cases of late-onset Pompe disease, and 30 suspected late-onset cases among 531,139 newborns. Lower GAA activity distinguished confirmed or suspected late-onset disease from carriers and pseudodeficiency at the group level, while CK, ALT, AST, and Hex4 had limited value for individual classification; early enzyme replacement therapy was followed by cardiac improvement in both reported infantile-onset cases.
papers.why: The population study validates a two-tier GAA activity and sequencing protocol for newborn detection of infantile and late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: Gene Therapy Developments for Pompe Disease.
papers.summary: This review reports that Pompe disease is caused by deficient acid alpha-glucosidase and identifies major limitations of lifelong enzyme replacement therapy, especially inadequate skeletal-muscle, respiratory, and CNS effects. It highlights substantial preclinical and emerging clinical evidence for AAV and lentiviral HSPC gene therapies, while emphasizing incomplete multisystemic correction, immunogenicity, biodistribution, and genotoxicity risks.
papers.why: The review summarizes existing Pompe disease gene-therapy platforms and optimized vector designs with preclinical or clinical translational evidence.

papers.title: Update of the Pompe variant database for the prediction of clinical phenotypes: Novel disease-associated variants, common sequence variants, and results from newborn screening.
papers.summary: The paper updates the Pompe disease GAA variant database with 226 newly identified disease-associated variants, 148 common non-disease-associated sequence variants, and variants detected through newborn screening whose clinical severity remains unknown. Selected common missense variants were functionally tested in COS-7 cells, and the database and accompanying assays are presented as resources for variant interpretation, molecular diagnosis, and prediction of genotype–phenotype relationships.
papers.why: The updated open-access database provides curated disease-associated GAA variants, benign variants, newborn-screening variants, phenotype data, and functional expression results for Pompe genetics.

papers.title: Disease modeling and lentiviral gene transfer in patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cells from late-onset Pompe disease patient.
papers.summary: The study generated three patient-specific induced pluripotent stem cell lines from one patient with late-onset Pompe disease and showed that they, particularly after cardiomyocyte differentiation, reproduced GAA deficiency, lysosomal glycogen accumulation, and lysosomal enlargement. Third-generation lentiviral GAA gene transfer increased GAA expression and activity and improved these abnormalities, although glycogen content was not fully normalized within 48 hours and the efficacy was not demonstrated clinically.
papers.why: The study creates Pompe-specific iPSC-derived cardiomyocytes and shows that lentiviral GAA rescue improves enzyme activity, glycogen accumulation, and lysosomal abnormalities.

papers.title: Three-dimensional tissue-engineered human skeletal muscle model of Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The paper establishes patient-derived 3D human skeletal muscle myobundles as an in vitro model of infantile-onset Pompe disease that reproduces GAA deficiency, glycogen accumulation, lysosomal enlargement, stress-dependent contractile deficits, and disease-associated transcriptional changes. Recombinant human GAA and AAV-mediated hGAA expression substantially restored enzyme activity and cleared glycogen but did not reverse stress-induced functional deficits, while producing only partial molecular rescue.
papers.why: The study develops a patient-derived human myobundle model, tests enzyme and gene replacement approaches, and provides a disease-specific transcriptomic signature for drug screening and mechanism studies.

papers.title: Newborn Screening for Pompe Disease in Illinois: Experience with 684,290 Infants.
papers.summary: Illinois statewide tandem mass spectrometry newborn screening identified 29 definitively diagnosed infants with Pompe disease among 684,290 screened, including 3 with infantile-onset and 26 with late-onset disease, with no reported affected infants missed. Early enzyme replacement therapy was associated with favorable short-term outcomes in the three treated infantile-onset cases, while the single treated late-onset case showed motor improvement but persistent weakness and required dose escalation.
papers.why: This report provides large-scale real-world evidence for an existing newborn-screening and diagnostic pathway for Pompe disease.

papers.title: Benefits of Prophylactic Short-Course Immune Tolerance Induction in Patients With Infantile Pompe Disease: Demonstration of Long-Term Safety and Efficacy in an Expanded Cohort.
papers.summary: In a retrospective cohort of 34 infants with infantile Pompe disease, short-course immune tolerance induction with rituximab, methotrexate, and IVIG initiated with alglucosidase alfa was associated with durable immune tolerance, preserved vaccination responses, and improved survival and ventilator-free outcomes compared with a historical ERT-monotherapy cohort. Treatment caused transient neutropenia and reversible mild AST elevation in some patients, while five patients developed infections; deaths were attributed to Pompe disease progression rather than immunomodulation.
papers.why: A 34-patient infantile Pompe cohort provides long-term safety and immunogenicity data for prophylactic immune tolerance induction before enzyme replacement therapy.

papers.title: Diagnosis and treatment of late-onset Pompe disease in the Middle East and North Africa region: consensus recommendations from an expert group.
papers.summary: This consensus statement reviews the diagnosis, treatment, and monitoring of late-onset Pompe disease and reports regional recommendations for the Middle East and North Africa. It identifies alglucosidase alfa as an established therapy that stabilizes or improves disease manifestations but is not curative, and describes several experimental approaches—including NeoGAA, BMN 701, chaperone therapy, and AAV-GAA gene delivery—with promising but still limited clinical evidence.
papers.why: The consensus document supplies practical diagnostic and treatment algorithms for late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: An immune tolerance approach using transient low-dose methotrexate in the ERT-naïve setting of patients treated with a therapeutic protein: experience in infantile-onset Pompe disease.
papers.summary: In a small observational cohort, transient low-dose methotrexate co-initiated with alglucosidase alfa enzyme replacement therapy was associated with predominantly low or absent sustained anti-rhGAA IgG antibody titers in treatment-naïve infantile-onset Pompe disease, compared with historical ERT-only controls. The protocol was feasible and reasonably tolerated, but two recipients developed intermediate or high-sustained titers, and larger controlled and longer-term studies are required.
papers.why: The study tests low-dose methotrexate as an immune-tolerance strategy during enzyme replacement therapy in CRIM-positive infantile Pompe disease.

papers.title: Late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) in Belgium: clinical characteristics and outcome measures.
papers.summary: In a Belgian cohort of 52 patients with late-onset Pompe disease, longitudinal data showed significant declines in 6-minute walk distance, MRC sum score, and forced vital capacity, whereas ActivLim score and 10-m walk time did not significantly change. The study also identified a long diagnostic delay, recurrent GAA variants, vascular abnormalities on brain imaging, and outcome measures suitable for clinical follow-up.
papers.why: Seven-year longitudinal data show that 6-minute walking distance, MRC sum score, and forced vital capacity are sensitive clinical outcome measures in late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: Lessons Learned from Pompe Disease Newborn Screening and Follow-up.
papers.summary: This six-year Missouri newborn-screening program diagnosed 46 children with Pompe disease, identified common GAA pseudodeficiency variants, and showed that age- and season-adjusted GAA cutoffs plus multi-enzyme quality assessment can reduce false-positive referrals. Early enzyme replacement therapy was associated with cardiac improvement and stable or improved development in most followed children with infantile-onset Pompe disease, although infusion reactions, adverse outcomes, loss to follow-up, and later-onset disease presenting in infancy remained important limitations.
papers.why: The report describes six years of operational experience with Pompe newborn screening and follow-up, including management of later-onset phenotypes and pseudodeficiency alleles.

papers.title: Cipaglucosidase Alfa: First Approval.
papers.summary: The paper reports that cipaglucosidase alfa plus miglustat is an approved long-term enzyme replacement therapy for adults with late-onset Pompe disease. Clinical studies showed reductions in muscle-damage and glycogen-accumulation biomarkers and potentially meaningful motor and respiratory improvements, although the combination did not demonstrate statistical superiority over alglucosidase alfa for the primary 6-minute walk distance endpoint.
papers.why: This paper reports the approval of cipaglucosidase alfa with miglustat as a long-term enzyme replacement therapy for adult late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: Newborn screening for Pompe disease in Italy: Long-term results and future challenges.
papers.summary: In 206,741 Italian newborns screened for Pompe disease, 11 were confirmed with pathogenic GAA variants; all three infants with infantile-onset disease who received early alglucosidase alfa had good overall outcomes, although one developed high-titer anti-rhGAA antibodies and persistent neurodevelopmental impairment. Urinary glucose tetrasaccharide and cardiac assessment rapidly separated infantile-onset from late-onset cases, while enzyme activity, genotype, and creatine kinase had important diagnostic or prognostic limitations.
papers.why: A seven-year screening program provides validated screening, prognostic biomarker, follow-up, and early-treatment data directly applicable to Pompe disease research.

papers.title: An analysis of Pompe newborn screening data: a new prevalence at birth, insight and discussion.
papers.summary: Direct newborn-screening data from 11,619,662 births estimated Pompe disease birth prevalence at 1:18,711, with the authors identifying this as a conservative minimum estimate. The analysis found no clear ancestry-based difference in total prevalence, although the proportions of infantile-onset and late-onset disease differed across regions.
papers.why: The paper provides a large same-disease newborn-screening dataset and a reusable statistical framework for reliable prevalence estimation.

papers.title: A nonsense mutation in the acid α-glucosidase gene causes Pompe disease in Finnish and Swedish Lapphunds.
papers.summary: The paper identifies the GAA c.2237G>A (p.W746*) nonsense mutation as the cause of Pompe disease in Finnish and Swedish Lapphunds and finds that the mutation is also present in Lapponian Herders. Affected dogs reproduce the clinical, pathological, and biochemical features of infantile-onset Pompe disease, supporting their use as large-animal models for gene-therapy research and carrier testing for disease eradication.
papers.why: The naturally occurring canine model genetically and clinically recapitulates infantile Pompe disease and is proposed for preclinical gene-therapy studies.

papers.title: Long-term follow-up of 17 patients with childhood Pompe disease treated with enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.summary: In a prospective 17-child cohort with non-classic Pompe disease, long-term enzyme replacement therapy was associated with significant improvements in 6MWT and QMFT outcomes, while strength remained statistically unchanged. Lung-function outcomes were variable and sitting FVC declined overall, with substantial individual differences in treatment response.
papers.why: Prospective seven-year data show group-level functional benefits from ERT in childhood Pompe disease and provide longitudinal muscle and lung outcome measures.

papers.title: Light and Shadows in Newborn Screening for Lysosomal Storage Disorders: Eight Years of Experience in Northeast Italy.
papers.summary: This eight-year observational newborn-screening study identified 16 newborns with Pompe disease, including three infantile-onset and 13 late-onset cases. Early urinary Glc4, cardiologic assessment, GAA molecular analysis, and CRIM assessment supported rapid classification and immediate treatment; alglucosidase alfa produced favorable outcomes in two patients but was associated with anti-rhGAA antibodies, psychomotor delay, and persistent cardiomyopathy in one CRIM-negative patient.
papers.why: The large multiscreen study demonstrates an operational newborn-screening workflow for detecting Pompe disease and initiating early treatment.

papers.title: The Latin American experience with a next generation sequencing genetic panel for recessive limb-girdle muscular weakness and Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The study found that including GAA in a targeted 10-gene next-generation sequencing panel identified pathogenic or likely pathogenic GAA genotypes and enabled molecular diagnosis in nine Latin American patients with suspected Pompe disease. Fluorometric GAA enzyme testing corroborated the diagnosis in tested siblings, although the convenience cohort, limited clinical follow-up, and inability of the panel to evaluate many variant classes constrained diagnostic completeness.
papers.why: The targeted panel successfully identified nine Pompe cases among 2,103 patients with proximal muscle weakness, supporting molecular differential diagnosis.

papers.title: CRISPR-Cas9 generated Pompe knock-in murine model exhibits early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and skeletal muscle weakness.
papers.summary: The paper develops a CRISPR-Cas9 Gaa c.1826dupA (p.Y609*) knock-in mouse and an isogenic C2C12 cell line that exhibit GAA deficiency, glycogen accumulation, impaired autophagy, early-onset hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and skeletal muscle weakness characteristic of infantile-onset Pompe disease. The knock-in strategy showed high on-target efficiency and no detectable genomic off-target activity, but the mice did not reproduce the early mortality of untreated infantile-onset Pompe disease.
papers.why: The paper reports a genome-edited murine model reproducing infantile Pompe cardiomyopathy and muscle weakness for therapeutic testing.

papers.title: Enzymatic diagnosis of Pompe disease: lessons from 28 years of experience.
papers.summary: This 28-year diagnostic study compared GAA enzymatic assays in leukocytes, fibroblasts, and dried blood spots for Pompe disease. Cultured skin fibroblasts measured with 4MUG provided the most reliable distinction between classic infantile and later-onset phenotypes, while leukocyte glycogen assays were vulnerable to GAA2 and Asian pseudodeficiencies and DBS testing produced false-negative results in this cohort.
papers.why: A large diagnostic cohort shows that fibroblast 4MUG GAA testing is the most reliable assay for confirming Pompe disease and excluding pseudodeficiency.

papers.title: An artificial intelligence-based approach for identifying rare disease patients using retrospective electronic health records applied for Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The study found that Symptoma's artificial intelligence could retrospectively screen 350,116 electronic health records for suspected Pompe disease, flagging 104 patients, of whom 19 remained clinically plausible after generalist and specialist review. The resulting phenotypes suggest that myopathy, muscle weakness, myalgia, scapula alata, and muscle hypotony discriminate clinically plausible patients from comparison cohorts, although the positive cohort was small and the approach had low reported specificity.
papers.why: The study applies an AI screening method to 350,116 EHRs and provides performance data for identifying suspected Pompe cases.

papers.title: Correction of oxidative stress enhances enzyme replacement therapy in Pompe disease.
papers.summary: The paper shows that oxidative stress is elevated in Pompe disease patient cells and Gaa-knockout mouse tissues and reduces the activity, uptake, processing, and lysosomal delivery achieved with recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase. Antioxidant co-treatment, particularly N-acetylcysteine or idebenone, improved enzyme correction in fibroblasts and selected tissues in mice, supporting oxidative-stress correction as an adjunct strategy for enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.why: Patient cells and a Pompe mouse model show that multiple antioxidants enhance enzyme activity and processing during recombinant human GAA treatment.

papers.title: Current status of newborn screening for Pompe disease in Japan.
papers.summary: A Japanese newborn-screening program combining dried-blood-spot GAA enzyme assays with GAA sequencing identified one patient with infantile-onset Pompe disease and seven individuals with potential late-onset Pompe disease. Early enzyme replacement therapy in the infantile-onset case was followed by improved hypotonia and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, but pseudodeficiency variants produced a high false-positive rate and the screening strategy did not definitively diagnose asymptomatic potential late-onset cases.
papers.why: The Japanese newborn-screening program reports feasibility, diagnostic findings, pseudodeficiency frequencies, and successful early treatment of infantile-onset disease.

papers.title: Pompe disease treatment with twice a week high dose alglucoside alfa in a patient with severe dilated cardiomyopathy.
papers.summary: This case report describes a 3-month-old boy with severe infantile-onset Pompe disease who received alglucosidase alfa at 40 mg/kg twice weekly for 21 infusions, followed by 40 mg/kg weekly. Cardiac function, biomarkers, respiratory independence, and developmental abilities improved without reported infusion adverse reactions, but the efficacy and safety of this high-frequency regimen remain uncertain because evidence is limited to one patient and treatment was concurrent with other cardiac care.
papers.why: The case report provides clinical outcome data for a high-dose alglucosidase alfa regimen in an infant with severe Pompe cardiomyopathy.

papers.title: Performance of the Four-Plex Tandem Mass Spectrometry Lysosomal Storage Disease Newborn Screening Test: The Necessity of Adding a 2nd Tier Test for Pompe Disease.
papers.summary: In 64,148 newborns screened with a four-plex tandem mass spectrometry lysosomal storage disease assay, 20 infants were referred for Pompe disease confirmation and six were confirmed. The study found that adding a second-tier acarbose-inhibition assay was necessary to distinguish Pompe disease from pseudodeficiency and reduce false-positive referrals while preserving timely referral of true positives.
papers.why: The study reports implementation and validation of a multiplex newborn-screening assay and shows that acarbose inhibition testing reduces Pompe false positives.

papers.title: Newborn Screening for 6 Lysosomal Storage Disorders in China.
papers.summary: This Shanghai cohort study found a birth prevalence of Pompe disease of 1 diagnosis in 16,702 live births among 50,108 newborns screened with tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) newborn screening. All 3 confirmed Pompe cases had later-onset disease and carried the GAA pathogenic variant c.2238G>C (p.Trp746Cys); the study also evaluated biochemical, genetic, and clinical confirmation methods and identified limitations related to GAA pseudodeficiency and incomplete genetic testing.
papers.why: The study validates an MS/MS newborn-screening workflow that identified and clinically characterized three newborns with Pompe disease.

papers.title: Novel GAA Variants and Mosaicism in Pompe Disease Identified by Extended Analyses of Patients with an Incomplete DNA Diagnosis.
papers.summary: Extended molecular analyses completed the DNA diagnosis of six suspected Pompe disease patients from four families by identifying three novel non-coding GAA variants and one case of mosaic segmental uniparental isodisomy. The study supports follow-up with exon-flanking RT-PCR, SNP array analysis, minigene analysis, quantitative RT-PCR, FISH, and related assays when routine GAA coding-region sequencing or biochemical findings are insufficient or discordant.
papers.why: Extended molecular assays resolved previously unexplained Pompe cases by identifying deletions, splice variants, and low-level genetic mosaicism.

papers.title: Immune Tolerance-Adjusted Personalized Immunogenicity Prediction for Pompe Disease.
papers.summary: The study reports that a personalized computational immunogenicity model, PIMA V3J, incorporated patient-specific GAA variants, HLA DR alleles, and predicted regulatory T-cell epitopes to identify CRIM-positive children at increased risk of high anti-rhGAA antibody titers. In vitro testing further showed that four GAA-derived peptides suppressed tetanus-toxoid–specific memory CD4+ T-cell proliferation and increased the regulatory-to-effector T-cell ratio, but clinical validation of both PIMA and these peptides remains necessary.
papers.why: The patient-data study develops and validates a computational method for predicting anti-drug antibody risk before alglucosidase alfa treatment.

papers.title: New Insights into Gastrointestinal Involvement in Late-Onset Pompe Disease: Lessons Learned from Bench and Bedside.
papers.summary: This clinical and mouse-model study shows extensive gastrointestinal pathology in Pompe disease, including glycogen accumulation throughout the gastrointestinal tract and frequent, burdensome gastrointestinal symptoms in adults with late-onset Pompe disease. PROMIS-GI measures and focused gastrointestinal histories can quantify these manifestations, while alglucosidase alfa enzyme replacement therapy shows tissue-level benefit in mice but little or inconsistent clinical improvement in patients, motivating therapies that more effectively target smooth muscle and neural components.
papers.why: The study combines a GAA-knockout mouse model, long-term ERT experiments, and patient PROMIS-GI outcomes to assess gastrointestinal disease in Pompe disease.

papers.title: Optimizing treatment outcomes: immune tolerance induction in Pompe disease patients undergoing enzyme replacement therapy.
papers.summary: In a prospective eight-patient cohort with CRIM-positive infantile-onset or late-onset Pompe disease, a six-month immune tolerance induction regimen combining bortezomib, rituximab, methotrexate, and intravenous immunoglobulin significantly reduced anti-drug antibody titers. The reduction was not accompanied by consistent biomarker normalization or demonstrable motor or respiratory improvement, and the small uncontrolled cohort, delayed treatment in some patients, infection events, and possible transient bortezomib-related neuropathy limit the findings.
papers.why: A prospective Pompe study shows that immune tolerance induction substantially reduces anti-ERT antibody titers and reports biochemical and clinical monitoring outcomes.

Normally, GAA is used by the body's cells to break down glycogen (a stored form of sugar) within specialized structures called lysosomes. In patients with Pompe disease, an excessive amount of glycogen accumulates and is stored in various tissues, especially heart and skeletal muscle, which prevents their normal function. papers.title: A Study to Evaluate the Safety, Pharmacokinetics, and Pharmacodynamics of DNL952 in Adult Participants With Late-Onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: This is a Phase 1, multicenter, open-label study to evaluate the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics (PK), and pharmacodynamics (PD) of DNL952 in adult participants with late-onset Pompe disease. The principal aim of this study is to obtain safety and tolerability data across varous dose levels of DNL952 in participants with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD).

papers.title: Late-Onset Treatment Study Extension Protocol

Normally, GAA is used by the body's cells to break down glycogen (a stored form of sugar) within specialized structures called lysosomes. The objective of this extension study is to assess the long-term safety and efficacy of alglucosidase alfa treatment

papers.title: Immune Tolerance Induction Study
papers.summary: An exploratory, open-labeled study of participants with Pompe disease, who had previously received Myozyme® (alglucosidase alfa) treatment, to evaluate the efficacy, safety and clinical benefit of 2 Immune Tolerance Induction (ITI) regimens in combination with Myozyme®. Eligible participants who were then receiving Myozyme® therapy were enrolled into the study, and were followed for a minimum of 18 months on-study (a 6-month ITI treatment module and a 12-month follow-up module on Myozyme® alone). Eligible participants were followed for a minimum of 18 months on treatment or, if a participant w

papers.title: AAV2/8-LSPhGAA (ACTUS-101) in Late-Onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: Open-label, ascending dose trial of ACTUS-101 administered intravenously.

papers.title: Avalglucosidase Alfa Extension Study
papers.summary:
Primary Objective:

Long-term safety and pharmacokinetics (PK) of avalglucosidase alfa

Secondary Objective:

Long-term effect of avalglucosidase alfa on pharmacodynamic variables

papers.title: Safety Study of Recombinant Adeno-Associated Virus Acid Alpha-Glucosidase to Treat Pompe Disease
papers.summary: Pompe disease is an inherited condition of acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA) deficiency resulting in lysosomal accumulation of glycogen in all tissues. Glycogen accumulation leads to muscle dysfunction and profound muscle weakness. A wide spectrum of disease is characteristic and the most severe patients have cardiorespiratory failure, often fatal in the first two years of life. Researchers have developed a way to introduce the normal GAA gene into muscle cells with the expectation that the GAA protein will be produced at levels sufficient to reduce glycogen accumulation. papers.title: Drug-drug Interaction Study
papers.summary: This study evaluates drug-drug interactions between AT2220 (duvoglustat) and recombinant human alpha-glucosidase (rhGAA, also known as alglucosidase alfa) in participants with Pompe Disease.

papers.title: Extension Study of Patients With Infantile-Onset Pompe Disease Who Were Previously Enrolled in Protocol AGLU01602

papers.title: Evaluation of Salbutamol as an Adjuvant Therapy for Pompe Disease

papers.title: Phase II Clinical Trial of Clenbuterol in Adult Patients With Pompe Disease
papers.summary: The goals of this study are to determine safety and efficacy with regard to motor function of oral clenbuterol in combination with ERT in subjects with LOPD

Normally, GAA is used by the body's cells to break down glycogen (a stored form of sugar) within specialized structures called lysosomes. In patients with Pompe disease, an excessive amount of glycogen accumulates and is stored in various tissues, especially heart and skeletal muscle, which prevents their normal function. The objective of this protocol is to provide enzyme replacement therapy with alglucosidase alfa on an expanded access

papers.summary:
This is an open-label, multicenter study of participants with late-onset Pompe disease naive to treatment with enzyme replacement therapy (ERT). The primary objective of this study is to evaluate glycogen clearance in muscle tissue samples collected pre and post alglucosidase alfa treatment in participants with Late-Onset Pompe disease.

The secondary objectives are to characterize the disease burden in participants with late-onset Pompe disease and explore imaging, histologic, and functional assessments in these participants and to explore potential plasma or urine biomarkers relative to late

papers.title: An Exploratory Study of the Safety and Efficacy of Prophylactic Immunomodulatory Treatment in Myozyme-naive Cross-Reacting Immunologic Material (CRIM[-]) Patients With Infantile-Onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary:
The purpose of this study was to evaluate the efficacy, clinical benefits and safety of a prophylactic immunomodulatory regimen given prior to first treatment with alglucosidase alfa (Myozyme®) in patients with infantile-onset Pompe disease.

The objectives were to assess the efficacy of a prophylactic immunomodulatory regimen given prior to first treatment with alglucosidase alfa, as assessed by anti-recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase (anti-rhGAA) antibody titers, and antibodies that inhibit the activity and/or uptake of alglucosidase alfa; to evaluate the clinical benefit as measured b

papers.title: A Pilot Study of Zavesca® in Patients With Pompe Disease and Infusion Associated Reaction
papers.summary:
Hypothesis: the effectiveness of treatment of Pompe disease with rhGAA enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) is limited at least in part because patients develop antibodies against the provided rhGAA enzyme. Treatment with Zavesca® prior to infusion may dampen or eliminate the anti-rhGAA immune response in patients receiving ERT, thereby allowing for greater ERT efficacy.

Treatment with Zavesca® before a enzyme replacement therapy (ERT) may decrease the severity of, or eliminate infusion associated reactions (IAR) in people with Pompe Disease receiving ERT.

papers.title: An Extension Study of S-606001 in Participants With Late-onset Pompe Disease (LOPD)
papers.summary:
The primary purpose of this study is to evaluate the long-term safety and tolerability profile of S-606001 in participants with LOPD.

Participants who completed other S-606001 studies (for example, NCT07123155), including participants in a S-606001 study whose allocated arm was terminated by the sponsor and who are willing to participate in this study, will be enrolled globally.

papers.title: Extension Study of Long-term Safety and Efficacy of Myozyme for a Single Patient With Pompe Disease Who Were Previously Enrolled in Genzyme Sponsored ERT Studies.
papers.summary: This extension study was to monitor the long-term safety and efficacy of rhGAA treatment in a single patient with infantile-onset Pompe disease who were previously treated with rhGAA in a Genzyme study.

papers.title: Study to Assess the Safety, Tolerability, PK and PD of ABX1100
papers.summary:
Study ABX1100-1001 is a first-in-human (FIH), phase 1 study to assess the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of a single ascending dose (SAD) and multiple doses (MD) of ABX1100 administered intravenously to healthy participants and patients with LOPD.

* Part A features a SAD study with a double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized design in NHVs involving 3 cohorts (A1-A3). This Part also includes a single dose, open-labeled cohort (A4) in NHVs which will commence after cohorts A1-3.
* Part B is a MD, double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized design in NHVs. The M

papers.title: Pharmacokinetics of Alglucosidase Alfa in Patients With Pompe Disease
papers.summary:
* The primary objective of this study was to characterize the pharmacokinetics (PK) of alglucosidase alfa manufactured at the 4000 L scale in participants who had a confirmed diagnosis of Pompe disease.
* A secondary objective of this study was to evaluate and explore the relationship between anti-recombinant human acid alpha-glucosidase antibody titers and the PK of alglucosidase alfa.

papers.title: Safety and Efficacy of Avalglucosidase Alfa in Patients With Non-classic Pompe Disease Aged ≥ 5 Years
papers.summary:
The goal of this clinical trial is to study the efficacy and safety of treatment with avalglucosidase alfa in patients with late onset Pompe disease that previously deteriorated on alglucosidase alfa.

The main question it aims to answer is:

* Is switching to avalglucosidase alfa in late-onset Pompe patients deteriorating on alglucosidase alfa safe?
* Is switching to avalglucosidase alfa in late-onset Pompe patients deteriorating on alglucosidase alfa potentially more effective?

Participants will switch to biweekly avalglucosidase alfa infusions (instead of alglucosidase alfa infusions) and

papers.title: A Study Comparing ATB200/AT2221 With Alglucosidase Alfa/Placebo in Adult Subjects With Late-onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: This is a phase 3 double-blind randomized study to study the efficacy and safety of intravenous ATB200 Co-administered with oral AT2221 in adult subjects with Late Onset Pompe Disease compared with Alglucosidase Alfa/placebo.

papers.title: Gene Transfer Study in Patients With Late Onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: This is a phase 1/2 open-label, ascending dose, multicenter clinical study to evaluate the safety and efficacy of AT845 in adult (aged ≥ 18 years) subjects, ambulatory or nonambulatory, with Late Onset Pompe Disease (LOPD).

papers.title: Safety and Efficacy of Albuterol in Individuals With Late-onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: In this study the study team proposes to investigate the efficacy of albuterol on motor function of individuals with Late Onset Pompe Disease (LOPD) who are receiving enzyme replacement therapy, given albuterol was well-tolerated in patients with Late Onset Pompe Disease.

papers.title: A Study to Evaluate the Efficacy and Safety of Alglucosidase Alfa Produced at the 4000 L Scale for Pompe Disease
papers.summary: The objective of this study was to evaluate the efficacy and safety of treatment with 4000 litre (L) alglucosidase alfa (Lumizyme®) in Pompe participants.

papers.title: VAL-1221 Delivered Intravenously in Ambulatory and Ventilator-free Participants With Late-Onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: This Phase I/II open-label, randomized, dose-escalation study will assess the safety, tolerability, pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and preliminary efficacy of VAL-1221 versus Myozyme®/Lumizyme® in participants with late-onset glycogen storage disease-II (GSD-II) (Pompe disease)

papers.title: Re-administration of Intramuscular AAV9 in Patients With Late-Onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: A recombinant AAV vector has been generated to carry the codon-optimized acid alpha-glucosidase (coGAA) gene expressed from a human desmin enhancer/promoter (DES). The proposed clinical trial is a within-participant, double-blind, randomized, phase I controlled study evaluating the toxicology, biodistribution and potential activity of re-administration of rAAV9-DES-hGAA injected intramuscularly into the TA. Nine participants (18 to 50-years old) who reside within the United States with Late-Onset Pompe Disease (LOPD) will be included. The goal of the immune modulation strategy is to ablate B-c

papers.title: Growth and Development Study of Alglucosidase Alfa
papers.summary: Pompe disease (also known as glycogen storage disease Type II) is a rare autosomal recessive metabolic muscle disease caused by the deficiency of acid α glucosidase (GAA), an enzyme that degrades lysosomal glycogen. As opposed to the exclusively cytoplasmic accumulation of glycogen that occurs in other glycogen storage disorders, Pompe disease is characterized by organelle bound (lysosomal) and extra-lysosomal accumulation of glycogen in many body tissues, ultimately leading to multisystemic pathology. The overall objective of this study was to evaluate the long-term growth and development of

papers.title: Treatment Frequency Reduction in Pompe Disease
papers.summary: The aim of this study is to assess if dosing frequency reduction of alglucosidase alfa 20 mg/kg once every 2 weeks to once every 4 weeks is safe and does not lead to increased progression of disease in a selected group of patients with late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: A Study to Assess the Long-term Safety and Efficacy of ATB200/AT2221 in Adult Subjects With Late-Onset Pompe Disease (LOPD)
papers.summary: This is a multicenter, international open-label extension study of ATB200/AT2221 in adult subjects with late-onset Pompe disease (LOPD) who completed Study ATB200-03.

papers.title: Safety and Efficacy of Recombinant Human Acid Alpha-Glucosidase in the Treatment of Classical Infantile Pompe Disease
papers.summary: Pompe disease is caused by a deficiency of a critical enzyme in the body called acid alpha glucosidase (GAA). Normally, GAA is used by the body's cells to break down glycogen (a stored form of sugar) within specialized structures called lysosomes. In infants with severe cases of Pompe disease (called Classical Infantile Pompe disease), an excessive amount of glycogen accumulates and is stored in various tissues, especially heart, skeletal muscle, and liver, which prevents their normal function. This study being conducted to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of recombinant human acid alpha-

papers.title: CPAP for Infantile Pompe Disease
papers.summary: Patients with infantile onset Pompe disease will be trained with continuous positive airway pressure to see if hypernasality can be improved.

papers.title: A Study of the Safety and Efficacy of rhGAA in Patients With Infantile-onset Pompe Disease
papers.summary: Pompe disease (also known as glycogen storage disease type II, "GSD-II") is caused by a deficiency of a critical enzyme in the body called acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA). Normally, GAA is used by the body's cells to break down glycogen (a stored form of sugar) within specialized structures called lysosomes. This study is being conducted to evaluate the safety and effectiveness of recombinant human acid alpha-gluc

papers.title: ZIP Study-OL Study of Safety, PK, Efficacy, PD, Immunogenicity of ATB200/AT2221 in Pediatrics Aged 0 to < 18 y.o. w/LOPD
papers.summary: This is a Phase 3, open-label, multicenter study to evaluate the safety, PK, efficacy, PD, and immunogenicity of Cipaglucosidase Alfa/Miglustat treatment in enzyme replacement therapy (ERT)-experienced and ERT-naïve pediatric subjects with Pompe disease, aged 0 to \< 18 years

papers.title: PEARL (PrEnAtal Enzyme Replacement Therapy for Lysosomal Storage Disorders)
papers.summary:
For detailed information, please view our study website: https://pearltrial.ucsf.edu/

The investigators aims to determine the the maternal and fetal safety and feasibility of in utero fetal enzyme replacement therapy in fetuses with Lysosomal Storage Diseases.

papers.title: Extension Study for Patients Who Have Participated in a BMN 701 Study
papers.summary: This is a Phase 2 open-label, multiple dose study of BMN 701 administered by IV infusion every 2 weeks (qow) to patients with late-onset Pompe disease.

papers.title: A Study of the Safety and Pharmacokinetics of rhGAA in Siblings With Glycogen Storage Disease Type II
papers.summary: GSD-II (also known as Pompe disease) is caused by a deficiency of a critical enzyme in the body called acid alpha-glucosidase (GAA). Normally, GAA is used by the body's cells to break down glycogen (a stored form of sugar) within specialized structures called lysosomes.
